q2147: In a capitalist economy goods go to those who can pay (purchasing power), not to those who need them most; in a socialist economy distribution follows need.
q2148: The Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) on financial inclusion recommended payments banks; the RBI licensed them in 2015.
Payments banks can take deposits up to ₹2 lakh but cannot lend.
q2150: PM-KUSUM stands for Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (2019); it supports solar pumps and solar power plants for farmers.
Run by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy.
q2151: Lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) is a strong reducing agent that reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols; sodium borohydride is too weak for acids.
Option A is misprinted as 'Lithium Aluminium Hydroxide'; the reagent meant is lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄).
q2152: Riccia, Marchantia and Funaria are bryophytes (liverworts and mosses); Ulva (sea lettuce) is a green alga.
Bryophytes are the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'.
q2153: Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which replaced CFCs, are used in air conditioners and refrigerators. They have no chlorine and do not harm the ozone layer, but they are powerful greenhouse gases.
The Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs.
q2154: Mizoram is called the 'molasses basin' because it is made of soft, unconsolidated rocks (NCERT Class 9).
Mizoram's hills are called the Lushai hills.
q2155: The Ganga–Brahmaputra (Sundarbans) delta in India and Bangladesh is the world's largest delta.
The Sundarbans is also the largest mangrove forest.
q2156: A dendritic drainage pattern looks like the branches of a tree; it forms on uniform rock, e.g. the Ganga plain rivers.
Radial: from a central high (Amarkantak); trellis: folded rocks; centripetal: into a basin.
q2157: Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are India's most widespread forests; they shed leaves in the dry season. Teak and sal are typical trees.
Moist deciduous: over 100 cm rain; dry deciduous: 70–100 cm.
q2158: Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and Mahapadma Nanda ruled Magadha. Suddhodana was the Shakya chief of Kapilavastu and the Buddha's father.
Magadha dynasties: Haryanka → Shishunaga → Nanda → Maurya.
q2159: The Tamil Bhakti saints, the Nayanars (Shiva) and Alvars (Vishnu), drew on the love and heroism ideals of Sangam literature (NCERT Class 7).
q2160: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.
He spent his last years at Kartarpur, on the Ravi.
q2161: Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmednagar; the Mughal empire declined rapidly after him.
He is buried at Khuldabad, near Aurangabad.
q2162: The Battle of Buxar was fought in 1764; the British beat Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.
It led to the Treaty of Allahabad (1765).
q2172: The Government of India Act, 1935 divided powers between the Centre and provinces in three lists: Federal, Provincial and Concurrent.
The Constitution's Seventh Schedule follows this pattern.
q2173: The Swaran Singh Committee was set up in 1976; on its recommendation the 42nd Amendment added Fundamental Duties (Article 51A).
q2174: Article 61 lays down the procedure for impeaching the President for violating the Constitution; it needs a two-thirds majority in both Houses.
q2175: The 84th Amendment (2001) froze the allocation of Lok Sabha seats to states and the delimitation of constituencies until the first census after 2026.
The 42nd Amendment had first frozen seats on the 1971 census.
q2176: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes is a constitutional body (Article 338). The NHRC, NCW and NCDRC are statutory bodies set up by Acts.
Constitutional = named in the Constitution; statutory = created by an Act.
q2179: Shoaib Akhtar of Pakistan bowled the fastest recorded delivery, 161.3 km/h, against England at the 2003 World Cup.
q2387: The Golden Temple in Amritsar is also called Sri Harmandir Sahib or Sri Darbar Sahib; Guru Arjan Dev completed it.
The Adi Granth was installed there in 1604.
q2388: Pongal is Tamil Nadu's harvest festival, thanking the Sun god for the harvest of rice, sugarcane and turmeric.
'Pongal' is also the sweet rice dish cooked that day.
q2389: The Bara Imambara in Lucknow was built by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula in 1784 and is famous for its maze, the Bhool Bhulaiya.
Rumi Darwaza stands next to it.
q2390: Mohiniyattam takes its name from Mohini, the enchantress form of Lord Vishnu.
q2391: The shehnai is a double-reed wind instrument, played at weddings and temples; the tabla is a drum and the jhanj cymbals.
Ustad Bismillah Khan made the shehnai famous.
q2392: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 is called the 'Economic Constitution of India'; it gave the public sector the leading role under the Second Plan.
It sorted industries into Schedules A, B and C.
q2393: Allahabad Bank, founded in 1865 at Allahabad and later headquartered in Kolkata, was one of India's oldest joint-stock banks; it merged into Indian Bank in 2020.
The oldest existing bank today is the State Bank of India lineage (1806).
q2394: In the April 2020 bank mergers Syndicate Bank merged into Canara Bank. Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India went into Punjab National Bank; Andhra and Corporation Banks into Union Bank.
12 public sector banks remain after the mergers.
q2396: The joint between the neck and head is a pivot joint, which lets the head turn side to side.
Ball and socket: shoulder; hinge: elbow, knee; fixed: skull.
q2397: Redworms (earthworms) have no teeth; they grind food in their gizzard (NCERT Class 6).
Birds also grind food in a gizzard.
q2398: Normal human body temperature is about 37°C (98.6°F).
q2399: Platelets help blood clot at a wound, plugging the cut.
RBC: oxygen; WBC: immunity; platelets: clotting.
q2400: The Kosi is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' because of its floods and frequent changes of course.
q2401: The Konkan coast is the stretch of the west coast from Mumbai to Goa, mostly in Maharashtra.
Gujarat → Konkan → Kannad → Malabar (north to south).
q2402: Barchans are crescent-shaped sand dunes; along with longitudinal sand ridges they cover the Thar desert (NCERT).
q2403: Saline soils are also called usara soils; they have too much sodium and magnesium salts, and gypsum is used to reclaim them.
Found in western Gujarat, the Sundarbans and Punjab–Haryana.
q2404: 'Silappadikaram', the Tamil epic about Kannagi and Kovalan, was composed by Ilango Adigal.
Its companion epic is 'Manimekalai' by Sattanar.
q2405: Panini (about 5th century BCE) wrote the 'Ashtadhyayi', the classic grammar of Sanskrit.
Patanjali wrote the Yoga Sutras and the Mahabhashya on Panini.
q2406: Firuz Shah Tughlaq ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1351 to 1388, succeeding Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
He founded Firozabad and the towns of Hisar and Jaunpur.
q2407: Raja Todar Mal was Akbar's finance (revenue) minister; he introduced the zabt (dahsala) land revenue system.
q2408: 72 delegates attended the first session of the Indian National Congress in Bombay in December 1885, presided over by W.C. Bonnerjee.
Held at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College.
q2413: The IMF was created at the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944 (in force from December 1945) and is headquartered in Washington, D.C.
IMF and World Bank = Bretton Woods twins.
q2416: Kolkata has India's first underwater metro, a tunnel under the Hooghly river on the East–West Metro line, opened in 2024.
Kolkata also had India's first metro (1984).
q2418: The United Kingdom has no single written constitution; its constitution is made of statutes, conventions and court decisions.
India's is the longest written constitution in the world.
q2419: The Supreme Court of India came into existence on 26 January 1950, when the Constitution came into force, replacing the Federal Court.
The Court was formally inaugurated two days later, on 28 January 1950; DSSSB's key uses 26 January, when it came into existence.
q2420: In Hargovind Pant v. Raghukul Tilak (1979) the Supreme Court held that a Governor's office is an independent constitutional office, not employment under the Central Government.
The Governor is appointed by the President (Article 155).
q2421: Article 74(1) says there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at its head to aid and advise the President.
74(2): courts cannot inquire into the advice given.
q2422: The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners hold office for six years or until age 65, whichever comes first.
The CEC is removed like a Supreme Court judge.
q2431: The Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) was built around 999 CE by the Chandela kings (NCERT Class 7).
Khajuraho temples are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
q2432: Jahangir built the Shalimar Bagh in Srinagar for Nur Jahan (1619) on the shore of the Dal Lake.
Nishat Bagh (also Srinagar) was built by Asaf Khan.
q2433: Puthandu, the Tamil New Year, falls on 14 April, the first day of the Tamil month Chithirai.
Vishu is Kerala's New Year on the same day.
q2434: The Modhera festival (Uttarardh Mahotsav) is held at the Modhera Sun Temple in Gujarat each January.
Modhera Sun Temple: Solanki king Bhima I, 1026.
The event is a classical dance festival, not a film festival as the question says.
q2435: Pandit Ramashreya Jha, a Hindustani vocalist and composer, wrote many bandishes under the pen name 'Ram Rang'.
A bandish is a fixed composition in a raga.
q2436: UPI, RuPay and IMPS were developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI); PhonePe is a private payment app that runs on UPI.
NPCI was set up in 2008 by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.
q2437: A truck driver provides a transport service, so he is in the tertiary (service) sector.
Farmer: primary; factory worker: secondary; driver: tertiary.
q2438: After the April 2020 merger of 10 public sector banks into 4, India has 12 public sector banks.
q2440: Beryllium (atomic number 4) has the electronic configuration 2, 2: two electrons in the K shell and two in the L shell.
q2441: Vinegar is a 5–8% solution of acetic acid in water.
Tamarind: tartaric acid; lemon: citric acid.
Strictly, vinegar has no IUPAC name of its own; the IUPAC name of acetic acid is ethanoic acid. DSSSB's key means acetic acid.
q2442: A chronic disease lasts a long time. Elephantiasis (lymphatic filariasis) is chronic, while cold, flu and appendicitis are acute.
Filariasis is spread by the Culex mosquito.
q2443: Plasma, the fourth state of matter, forms when a gas is given so much energy that its atoms are ionised; stars and neon signs contain plasma.
Solid, liquid, gas, plasma (and Bose–Einstein condensate).
q2445: Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai hills of Kerala is the highest peak of the Peninsular plateau.
q2446: Meanders, the large bends of a river, form in its mature stage on flat plains where lateral erosion dominates.
q2447: The Andaman and Nicobar group in the Bay of Bengal has about 572 islands and islets (NCERT).
The Lakshadweep group in the Arabian Sea has 36 islands.
q2448: Evidence of rice (husk) has been found at the Harappan sites of Lothal and Rangpur in Gujarat.
q2449: Ashoka succeeded his father Bindusara as Mauryan emperor (about 268 BCE).
q2450: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah was a powerful noble at the court of Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar; he later founded the Hyderabad state (1724) (NCERT Class 7).
Hyderabad's rulers were called the Nizams.
q2452: The Mahalwari system was proposed by Holt Mackenzie (1822) and applied in the North-West Provinces, Punjab and Central India; revenue was settled with the village (mahal) as a whole.
Permanent Settlement: Cornwallis; Ryotwari: Thomas Munro and Alexander Read.
q2453: Dr Shankar Dayal Sharma was the ninth President of India (1992–97); before that he was Vice-President.
Presidents in order: Venkataraman → S.D. Sharma → K.R. Narayanan.
q2455: The World Meteorological Organization (a UN agency, 1950) is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.
q2457: The Shaurya Chakra, a peacetime gallantry award, can be given to both military personnel and civilians.
Peacetime order: Ashoka Chakra → Kirti Chakra → Shaurya Chakra.
q2460: World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February, marking the Ramsar Convention signed on that day in 1971.
q2462: The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6–14.
It also added the 11th Fundamental Duty (Article 51A(k)).
q2463: 'Police' and 'public order' are State List subjects in the Seventh Schedule.
q2464: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction over disputes between the Centre and states, or between states.
q2465: Bodo, a tribal language of Assam, was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Amendment (2003), with Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.
Santhali, another tribal language, was added in the same amendment.
q2466: The idea of Fundamental Duties was borrowed from the constitution of the former USSR.
Also from the USSR: the ideals of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble.
q2467: Sushil Kumar is a wrestler and India's only individual athlete with two Olympic medals in wrestling (bronze 2008, silver 2012).
q2468: The PGA Championship is one of golf's four men's major championships.
Golf majors: Masters, PGA Championship, US Open, The Open.
